issues.failure_explanation: The final big-O prefactors are built from $C_f,C_g,C_s,C_o$, which themselves depend on $\sigma$. Thus the proof does not establish the displayed explicit dependence consisting only of a $\sigma$-independent deterministic term plus a $\sigma^{1/2}$ stochastic term. It establishes, at best, the same powers of $T$ with additional unspecified noise dependence hidden in the constants.

failure_location.quote: Both variants achieve a noise-adaptive convergence rate of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2}+\sigma^{1/2} T^{-1/4})$ for the average gradient norm, where $\sigma$ is the noise level.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either weaken the advertised guarantee to acknowledge noise-dependent hidden constants, or redo the estimates so that all hidden constants are uniform in $\sigma$ and expose the full noise dependence.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed quantitative noise adaptivity, including comparisons across noise levels, is unsupported. The separate zero-variance rate may still survive if all other proof defects are repaired.
issues.title: Advertised noise dependence is hidden inside the proof constants
issues.why_classification: Weakening the claim abandons a central advertised guarantee, while preserving it requires a substantially different uniform analysis rather than a local edit.

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed equality drops the cross term between $\z_t$ and the stochastic-gradient noise. For OptEMA-M, $\alpha_t=\rho_t^{-1/2}$ depends on the current gradient $g_t=\nabla f(x_t;\xi_t)$, and $\z_t$ also contains $\alpha_t$. Consequently unbiasedness of $g_t$ does not make that cross term vanish. The proof treats $\alpha_t$ as predictable even though the algorithm makes it current-sample dependent.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must either redesign the coefficient to be predictable or provide a new bias/correlation analysis for the current-sample-dependent coefficient.
issues.overall_effect: The basic OptEMA-M tracking recursion and the entire convergence chain built from it are unsupported.
issues.title: Current-sample-dependent EMA weight invalidates the tracking-error cancellation
issues.why_classification: The defect occurs in the central stochastic estimator recursion. Repairing it requires changing the algorithm or supplying new proof architecture for an adaptive, biased weighting mechanism.

issues.failure_explanation: Lemma \ref{lemma:bound:eee:1} supplies only an inequality after expectation, so it does not imply the pointwise relation $\|s_t\|^2\leq\|s_{t-1}\|^2+B_t$ used in step 2, especially with a random multiplier depending on the trajectory. Independently, the stated bound on $\gamma_t$ gives $\gamma_t\mu(1+\tau_t)^2\leq2\alpha_t$, not the $2\gamma_t\mu(1+\tau_t)^2\leq\alpha_t$ needed to replace $-\alpha_t\|s_{t-1}\|^2$ by the displayed negative term.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a new conditional or pathwise tracking argument with a valid coefficient balance is required.
issues.overall_effect: The cumulative weighted tracking-error estimate is unproved, so all later OptEMA-M objective, gradient, and convergence estimates that use it are unreliable even if the preceding tracking lemma were repaired.
issues.title: Weighted tracking bound uses an unavailable pathwise recursion and a false coefficient comparison
issues.why_classification: The failed contraction is the main mechanism used to sum tracking errors; repairing it requires a replacement argument rather than local algebra.

issues.failure_explanation: The available estimate controls each $\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2$, but the proof replaces the random sum inside a logarithm by an expression involving the random maximum of the objective values without a pathwise inequality. It then replaces that random maximum by a deterministic sequence $A_t$ defined using expectations. Neither substitution follows from the stated bounded-variance assumption. The OptEMA-V proof repeats the same invalid transition.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the random-max argument with a valid Jensen-and-deterministic-maximum analysis, and re-establish the resulting circular logarithmic bound separately for each variant.
issues.overall_effect: The logarithmic expected objective and stochastic-gradient bounds used throughout both analyses are not established by the presented proofs.
issues.title: Objective boundedness proofs substitute expectation bounds inside random maxima and logarithms
issues.why_classification: A contained but nontrivial reworking of the expectation and circular-bound argument may preserve logarithmic expected bounds without changing the algorithms or headline rates.

issues.failure_explanation: First, $\mathbb E[\max_i X_i]\leq\max_i\mathbb E[X_i]$ is false; the inequality goes in the opposite direction in general. More broadly, Lemmas \ref{lemma:G:bound} and \ref{lemma:G:bound:2} claim only expected second-moment bounds, but later proofs use them as almost-sure bounds on every $g_t$, on $\tau_T=\max_t\|g_t\|$, and on objective values. Bounded variance permits unbounded stochastic gradients and supplies no such pathwise control.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, the proofs need new maximal-moment or truncation arguments under bounded variance, or the paper must impose an almost-sure bounded-gradient condition.
issues.overall_effect: The unweighted tracking estimate and the main cumulative-gradient estimates for both variants fail under the advertised bounded-variance-only regime.
issues.title: Expected second-moment bounds are repeatedly used as pathwise bounded-gradient guarantees
issues.why_classification: Adding bounded gradients would withdraw a central advertised assumption advantage, while retaining bounded variance alone requires new probabilistic proof architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: The replacement of $g_t$ by $\nabla f(x_t)$ is made only after taking expectation. The proof then treats the resulting relation as a pathwise recurrence for $\Theta_t$, unrolls it, and multiplies it by $\gamma_t$. But $\gamma_t$ depends on $\tau_t$ and $m_t$, hence on the current sample $g_t$; unbiasedness does not imply cancellation after multiplication by this correlated random stepsize. An unconditional expected recurrence cannot be promoted to the pathwise inequality used in the descent proof.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a new conditional analysis must retain the dependence between the current stochastic gradient and the adaptive stepsize, or the algorithm must use predictable statistics.
issues.overall_effect: The foundational OptEMA-V descent inequality and all convergence results based on it are unsupported.
issues.title: OptEMA-V takes expectation before multiplying by a current-sample-dependent stepsize
issues.why_classification: This invalidates the principal descent mechanism for the entire OptEMA-V analysis and requires new stochastic proof architecture or an algorithmic redesign.
